questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prokaryotic cells lack membrane-bound organelles.
questions.stem: A field survey turns up a microbe with no nucleus and no internal membranes; explain why such cells manage without those compartments.

answer.exemplar: Prokaryotic cells keep their reactions in the cytoplasm and on the cell membrane, whose folds and respiratory enzymes replace the energy-releasing membranes that eukaryotes house inside. Their simpler arrangement still supports diffusion, protein synthesis and respiration, and it allows very fast growth.

questions.explanation: Prokaryotes run metabolic pathways in the cytoplasm and on the plasma membrane, which carries the electron transport chain in place of internal membranes. That works, but limits compartmentalisation.
questions.hint: Their membranes and cytoplasm carry out the work.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain the significance of a cell's genetic material being free-floating.
questions.stem: A survey sample shows genetic material as a single circular loop with no surrounding membrane; explain what this arrangement allows.

answer.exemplar: A circular chromosome free in the cytoplasm, without a nuclear envelope, can be used directly to make messenger RNA, so transcription and translation happen in the same compartment and can be coupled. questions.explanation: With no nuclear membrane, transcription and translation are coupled and ribosomes can begin working on messenger RNA immediately. That speed suits organisms that grow and divide very quickly.
questions.hint: No nuclear barrier means translation can start at once.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how compartmentalisation supports a larger cell.
questions.stem: A survey compares a microbe with a nucleus-free cell and a larger cell with membrane-bound organelles; explain why the larger cell can work more efficiently.

answer.exemplar: Compartmentalisation lets each reaction run in the conditions it needs, with digestive enzymes isolated in lysosomes so they do not digest the rest of the cell, and respiration confined to mitochondria supplying ATP where it is used. The larger cell can therefore run many incompatible processes at once.

questions.explanation: Internal compartments give each process its own conditions, protect the cell from its own enzymes and allow incompatible reactions to run together, supporting larger cells with more varied jobs.
questions.hint: Compartments let incompatible reactions run together.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain why prokaryotes have a simpler cell structure.
questions.stem: A survey isolates a tiny cell with a cell wall, a plasma membrane and scattered ribosomes but nothing else inside; explain why nothing else is needed.

answer.exemplar: All the essential jobs can be done without separate compartments: metabolism runs in the cytoplasm, the plasma membrane carries the respiratory chain and regulates entry, and ribosomes build protein. questions.learningObjective: Explain how cell structure relates to the size of an organism.
questions.stem: A survey finds a single cell reaching 3 millimetres across; explain how a prokaryotic cell could manage that size.

answer.exemplar: A bacterium that large would need a surface that can serve a huge cytoplasm, so it might hold its DNA in several copies and spread metabolic enzymes across internal membrane folds and sacs. questions.explanation: Very large prokaryotes compensate with extra DNA copies and folded internal membranes, making up for missing compartments. A eukaryotic cell of the same size shows far more internal organisation.
questions.hint: Extra DNA copies and membrane folds help offset it.

questions.subject: BIOLOGY
questions.learningObjective: Explain how DNA replication works in a prokaryotic cell.
questions.stem: A survey sample divides in 20 minutes with a single circular chromosome; explain how its genetic material is copied.

answer.exemplar: The circular chromosome is anchored to the cell membrane, and as the cell grows the two attachment points separate while the DNA is copied in both directions from a single origin. questions.explanation: A single circular chromosome replicates from one origin, with the halves moving apart as the cell elongates, so each daughter receives one copy. A single copy makes mutation and gene transfer easier.
questions.hint: One chromosome, one origin, two copies.
